questions.question: Explain why South Africa's energy must be actively managed, naming the three pressures, and define the concept pair — greener economy and sustainable lifestyles — together with the master idea that links them.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa runs an energy-hungry, coal-dependent economy — about eight in ten units of electricity are coal-made — and three pressures make management compulsory. Supply: the load-shedding years proved demand can overwhelm a fragile system, and the fastest cure is trimming and shifting demand within months rather than building a station over a decade. Climate and trade: the country carries international climate commitments while trading partners introduce carbon border taxes, so goods manufactured with dirty electricity — steel, wine, citrus — pay penalties at foreign borders. Equity: poor households spend a punishing share of income on energy and clinics and schools fail without reliable power, so wasted energy is development thrown away. A greener economy is one that keeps growing while its resource consumption and emissions fall — prosperity unhooked from pollution — with energy as its main lever; sustainable lifestyles are the same idea at household scale, ways of living the whole population could copy without wrecking the resource base. Linking them is energy efficiency — the same service from fewer units — nicknamed the invisible power station, because deleting a station's worth of demand is faster, cheaper and cleaner than building one, captured in the champion sentence: the unit of electricity never used is the cheapest and cleanest there is.

questions.question: Compare the responsibilities of government and business in managing South Africa's energy toward a greener economy, giving specific tools for each.
questions.expected_answer: Government holds the instruments nobody else has. Planning: the Integrated Resource Plan schedules coal retirements and the solar, wind, storage, gas and nuclear capacity to be procured by which year, while auction rounds contract renewable producers and unbundling creates an independent transmission company so many generators compete on shared wires. Pricing and tax: Africa's first carbon tax charges emitters per tonne of carbon dioxide, levies fund efficiency programmes, and time-of-use tariffs reward off-peak consumption. Rules and standards: building regulations require energy performance in new buildings, appliance labels reveal running costs, and minimum standards remove the greediest appliances from sale. Direct delivery: subsidised solar water heaters and efficient lighting for low-income homes, free basic electricity, and the Just Energy Transition Partnership channelling tens of billions of dollars into grid building, retraining and green industry — plus leading by example through its own buildings and fleets. Business, which consumes most of the country's energy, manages through energy audits that trace waste — compressed-air leaks, worn motors, uninsulated pipes — and rank fixes by payback, typically finding double-digit savings; through self-generation, covering roofs and land with photovoltaic panels and building wind and solar farms of hundreds of megawatts, with wheeling delivering power across the grid between distant sites; through responding to supply-chain pressure, since carbon footprints are taxed at European borders and screened by lenders, making clean energy a passport to markets; and through honesty — measurable baselines, targets and audited results rather than greenwashing.

questions.question: Assess what individuals can realistically contribute to sustainable lifestyles, ranking the household actions by size and explaining both the citizen layer and the honest limits of individual action.
questions.expected_answer: Ranked by size: first the geyser, the hungriest appliance at around 40 per cent of a typical bill — thermostat down to sixty degrees, tank and pipes insulated, a timer fitted, and ultimately a solar water heater or heat pump handing the job to the sun; then lighting, the cheapest win, since an LED gives the same light for about a tenth of the electricity and lasts years; then cooking and warmth — lids on pots, pressure cookers and microwaves for small jobs, sealing draughts and warming the person rather than the room; then appliances — energy labels consulted before buying, machines run full, standby power cut at the wall; and transport — lift clubs, buses, taxis and walking, because petrol is energy too and often the largest saving available. Above the consumer sits the citizen layer: shifting flexible chores off the six-o'clock peak flattens demand for the whole grid, rooftop panels and solar geysers turn homes into micro power stations, and supporting transmission lines, renewable plants and transition plans in public processes is energy management with a citizen's voice, because infrastructure is only built where communities accept it. The honest limit: no single household can decarbonise a coal grid — but the evening peak is literally the sum of household choices made in the same hour, and the load-shedding years proved the sum responds when millions adjust; a sustainable lifestyle means keeping your own term in that sum small.
